sens: One who escapes death in battle or disaster
What remains after destruction or loss
One who stays alive when all others perish
H8300.detail:
1. A survivor is a person who escapes death during a battle or disaster. It is one who comes out alive when others are killed. In Joshua 8:22, the people of Ai are defeated "without leaving a survivor," meaning that none of them managed to flee or remain alive.
2. The word also refers to what remains of a people or community after a terrible ordeal. It is a remnant, a fraction spared from misfortune. In Jeremiah 31:2, God speaks of "those who escaped the sword," a small group of survivors amidst general destruction.
3. Sometimes the word simply expresses the idea that something is not destroyed, that it remains when everything else disappears. In Job 20:21, the text says that nothing "escaped" the greed of the rich: nothing survived in the face of his avarice.
H8300.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to remain" or "to subsist." It designates what remains when the rest is annihilated. The same root produces words that express the idea of what persists, of what does not disappear. It is a concrete word: it speaks of those who remain alive when others are dead.
H8300.emploi: The word appears 28 times in the Bible, mostly in the historical books (Joshua, Judges, Kings) and the prophets (Jeremiah, Isaiah). It is very common in accounts of conquest wars: Israel defeats its enemies "without leaving a survivor" (Joshua 8:22, 10:33, 11:8). The prophet Jeremiah uses it to speak of the exiles who escape the sword and the siege (Jeremiah 31:2, 42:17). In Lamentations and Joel, it evokes the small remnant that survives after the catastrophe. Job uses it to say that nothing escapes certain powers.
H8300.portee: The word survivor is important for the biblical theology of the remnant. The Bible shows that even in the midst of destruction and judgment, God preserves a small number of faithful. These survivors are the bearers of hope and God's promise for the future. Understanding this term helps the reader see how God acts in history: He does not destroy everything; He allows a remnant to persist through which His plan continues.

sens: Place name or landmark on the border of the tribe of Zebulun
H8301.detail: Sarid is a place name or geographical landmark mentioned during the division of the promised land among the tribes of Israel. It is located on the border of Zebulun, in northern Israel, and serves as a boundary or territorial marker in the description of tribal borders.
H8301.origine: The Hebrew name Sarid carries the meaning of "survivor" or "remnant" (from the root שׁרד, which evokes the idea of remaining, of subsisting). This type of place name was common in ancient Israel: some places were named after people, events, or remarkable natural features. It is not certain that this name directly evokes an event of survival; it may also refer to a particularity of the site or to a forgotten local tradition.
H8301.emploi: Sarid appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Joshua, during the description of the borders of the tribe of Zebulun (Joshua 19:10-12). In these passages, it is mentioned as a landmark from which the territorial limits of Zebulun are defined: the border "turned" or "extended" from Sarid to other places like Kisloth-Tabor, Dabrath, and Japhia. These very precise enumerations of boundary points constituted the biblical way of delineating the territories assigned to each tribe.

sens: hand-thrown projectile weapon
sharp projectile intended to pierce
instrument of war or hunting
H8302A.detail:
1. The javelin is a hand-thrown weapon, a kind of spear or dart that is thrown at an opponent or prey to strike from a distance. It is a pointed and lightweight weapon, different from the sword which is used in close combat. In Job 41:17, the poet lists all the warrior's efforts — the sword, the javelin, the breastplate — to show that none can harm Leviathan, this invulnerable monster: the javelin does nothing.
2. The word more broadly designates any pointed weapon thrown from a distance, whether it is a small dart or a larger spear. The image is that of a weapon that flies and pierces.
H8302A.origine: The Hebrew word shirya comes from a root that evokes the idea of throwing or projecting. It is a rare word in biblical Hebrew, related to other terms of weaponry and combat. Its equivalent in medieval French would be the javelin, a weapon very common before the bow.
H8302A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 41:17, in the description of Leviathan. The poet accumulates images of terrifying weapons — sword, javelin, breastplate — to show the total helplessness of warriors against this superhuman and invincible creature. This context suggests that the javelin is a formidable weapon of the ancient warrior, but remains insignificant in the face of divine power embodied in the monster.
H8302A.portee: This passage reminds us that, in the face of God's power, the most formidable human forces — even the complete arsenal of the warrior — are worthless. The javelin symbolizes the arsenal of the human warrior: learning that it is useless against Leviathan comforts the believer and invites him to place his trust only in the Lord, not in his own strength.

sens: metal protective garment worn by soldiers to defend their chest and vital organs
key element of the military equipment of an organized army
H8302B.detail:
1. The breastplate is a combat garment made of metal or metal scales, worn on the chest to protect the heart and lungs from blows. Goliath wore a very heavy one, made of bronze scales weighing five thousand shekels (1 Samuel 17:5); Saul offered one to David before his duel (1 Samuel 17:38). It is a defensive weapon, a sign of a well-equipped and experienced soldier.
2. The breastplate also designates, by extension, the complete war equipment of a disciplined army. King Uzziah had breastplates made for his entire army alongside shields, spears, and helmets (2 Chronicles 26:14); during the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem, Nehemiah's men stood ready, armed with breastplates and spears (Nehemiah 4:16). The breastplate thus becomes a symbol of organized strength and preparation for battle.
H8302B.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁרְיוֹן (shiryon) likely comes from a root related to the idea of rows or composition — which evokes the structure of scales or plates that make up this armor. The word appears mainly in contexts of organized warfare (kings, structured armies), always to designate this metal protection of the soldier. It is a technical vocabulary of military life.
H8302B.emploi: The breastplate appears 7 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, exclusively in accounts of war or military preparation. It first has a concrete and tactical importance: in the duel between David and Goliath (1 Samuel 17), the giant's breastplate symbolizes his apparent warrior superiority, while the one offered to David remains foreign to the young shepherd. It also comes into play in war wounds: when an archer strikes the king of Israel (Ahab) at the gap in the breastplate (1 Kings 22:34; 2 Chronicles 18:33), it marks the flaws even in a protection reputed to be solid. Finally, in contexts of building a strong army (Uzziah) or civil defense (Nehemiah), the breastplate becomes a sign of power and organized discipline.
H8302B.portee: The breastplate reminds us that material protection has its limits: even the most impressive armor (that of Goliath) can be defeated by faith (David), and even the best warrior can be wounded at the gap in his armor. In the story of salvation, this image also prepares the language of Paul in Ephesians 6:14, who speaks of the "breastplate of righteousness" — reminding us that the true protection of the believer comes not from metal, but from integrity and a righteous life in Christ.

sens: Name that the Sidonians gave to Mount Hermon
Mountain range of the Levant, with snowy and majestic peaks
H8303.detail:
1. Sirion is the local name used by the Sidonians (inhabitants of Sidon, a major Phoenician coastal city) to refer to Mount Hermon. In Deuteronomy 3:9, Moses specifies this variant of the name: while the local peoples call it Sirion, the Amorites call it Senir. It is a border mountain between the conquered lands and neighboring regions, well known to the peoples of the Levant.
2. In Psalm 29:6, Sirion represents a gigantic and imposing mountain, a symbol of natural power. The psalmist describes it leaping like a young buffalo under the power of the Lord's voice: it is the image of a mountain so majestic that it seems animated by an almost living force.
H8303.origine: The name "Sirion" comes from a Semitic root related to the idea of "armor" or "armored," perhaps evoking the rocky and steep slopes of the mountain, which resemble armor. It is another name for the same massif that the Hebrews called Hermon (חֶרְמוֹן), and that some neighboring peoples also named Senir. These name variants reflect the geographical and strategic importance of this mountain for the different populations of the Levant.
H8303.emploi: Sirion appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Deuteronomy 3:9, during the account of the conquest, Moses uses this name to accurately identify the border mountain, demonstrating his knowledge of the local geography and the different names used. In Psalms 29:6, the psalmist invokes Sirion as a symbol of natural majesty that responds to the creative power of God. These two uses attest that Sirion was a well-known and established name for this mountain, particularly among the peoples of northern Levant.

sens: Secretary of King David
High priest under King Zedekiah
Spiritual leader at the time of the fall of Jerusalem
H8304G.detail:
1. The name Seraja first designates the secretary or scribe of King David, the one who kept the records and wrote the official documents of the kingdom (2 Samuel 8:17). It is a position of trust, close to royal power.

2. The same name or a homonym also designates a high-ranking priest, son of Azariah, who was the high priest during the time of King Zedekiah of Judah, just before the capture of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar. He was the one who led the worship in the temple during one of the darkest hours of Israel's history.

3. Several other Seraja appear in the history of the return from exile after Babylon: priests, Levites, heads of priestly families. The name regularly recurs among the servants of the restored temple.
H8304G.origine: The name Seraja literally means "Jehovah is sovereign" or "the Eternal reigns": it combines the divine name (Yah, for Jehovah) and a verb indicating authority and governance. It is a typical theophoric name of the Israelite period, placing the bearer under divine sovereignty. Several different characters have borne this name throughout Israel's history, particularly after the exile.
H8304G.emploi: Seraja is the name of at least twelve different individuals in biblical history, from the time of the united monarchy to after the Babylonian exile. The Bible notably mentions him in 2 Samuel 8:17, where he appears as David's secretary, a key position in royal administration. The same name recurs in the genealogies of the priests and Levites who returned from captivity with Zerubbabel, and in accounts of spiritual and political crisis. This repetition of the name shows its importance in the Israelite priestly families.
H8304G.portee: The name Seraja, which means "the Eternal reigns," reminds us that even in positions of political or spiritual power, Israelite leaders recognized divine sovereignty over their functions. For the Christian reader, this name invites us to see that all true service of the king—whether civil or religious—must be rooted in the confession that God, the Eternal, is the true master.

sens: High priest of Judah at the time of King Zedekiah and the fall of Jerusalem
Father of Ezra the scribe
Levitical ancestor of a priestly lineage
H8304H.detail:
1. Seraja is the high priest of Judah in the final days of the kingdom before the capture of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar. He is arrested and executed along with the main temple officials (2 Kings 25:18 and Jeremiah 52:24).
2. He is the father of Ezra, the great scribe and priest who will return from exile to restore the law and worship in Jerusalem (Ezra 7:1).
3. He belongs to a significant line of Levitical priests: son of Azariah, father of Jehozadak, ancestor of generations of priests who served before the exile (1 Chronicles 6:14) and continued after (Nehemiah 11:11).
H8304H.origine: The name Seraja means "God is Master" or "Jehovah is Master." It comes from two Hebrew elements: Sarah (lord, prince) and Yah (God). It is a common theophoric name among priests and high-ranking individuals, expressing that God reigns over their lives. Several men bear this name in the Old Testament, all associated with important functions.
H8304H.emploi: Seraja is primarily mentioned as the high priest at the time of the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. The parallel texts of 2 Kings 25:18 and Jeremiah 52:24 report his arrest and execution during the city's capture. He is best known as the father of the great scribe Ezra (Ezra 7:1), who played a decisive role in the restoration of Judah after the exile. His genealogy is preserved in 1 Chronicles 6:14 to show the continuity of the priestly lineage up to the exile, and in Nehemiah 11:11 where a descendant bearing the same name figures among the temple officials after the return from exile.
H8304H.portee: The figure of Seraja reminds us that even in the most severe moments of judgment, God preserves a line of faithfulness. His son Ezra becomes the instrument of a major spiritual restoration after the exile. The continuity of his priestly descent shows how God maintains His covenant and worship through the gravest crises. It is a lesson of hope for the people of God: judgment is never the end.

sens: Judahite military leader at the time of the fall of Jerusalem
Son of Thanhumeth of Nethophah
H8304I.detail: 1. Seraja is a military leader who, after the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar, goes with his men to Gedaliah, the governor that the king of Babylon had established over Judah. He represents the last Judahite military leaders who accept Babylonian authority and seek an arrangement. 2. He is the son of Thanhumeth, an inhabitant of Nethophah (a locality in Judah). This lineage places him within a Judahite family from this region and distinguishes him from other characters of the same name in the Bible.
H8304I.origine: The name Seraja means "Jehovah is master" or "Jehovah governs": it combines the divine name YHWH (transcribed Jehovah) and a root that expresses royal dominion or authority. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing the confidence that God reigns over all things. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament, including priests and scribes.
H8304I.emploi: Seraja is mentioned exactly twice in the Bible, in two parallel passages recounting the same event. In 2 Kings 25:23 and Jeremiah 40:8, he is seen among the military commanders who come to submit to Gedaliah after the capture of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. These two accounts, one in royal history and the other in the words of the prophet Jeremiah, show Seraja's political and military role in the final days of the independent kingdom of Judah. His appearance in these two sources underscores the importance of this turning point for Israel.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, son of Kenaz and brother of Othniel
Father of Joab, founder of the valley of workers
H8304J.detail:
1. Seraja is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned at the beginning of the genealogy of the people of Israel before the monarchy. He is presented as the son of Kenaz and the brother of Othniel, important figures in Judean history (1 Chronicles 4:13). His name means "the Lord is master" or "God reigns".
2. Seraja is the father of Joab, an ancestor who took his name from a region called "the valley of workers" because its inhabitants practiced crafts. This lineage shows how certain families of Judah were associated with specific places and professions (1 Chronicles 4:14).
H8304J.origine: The name Seraja comes from the Hebrew שְׂרָיָה (serayah), composed of two elements: שַׂר (sar, "chief", "master") and יָהּ (yah, abbreviation of the name of God "Yahweh"). It thus means "Yahweh is master" or "the Lord reigns". This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common among the ancient Hebrews to express their trust in divine sovereignty.
H8304J.emploi: Seraja is a character in the genealogy of Judah, mentioned only twice in the provided references, in verses 13 and 14 of chapter 4 of 1 Chronicles. He appears in the context of the pre-monarchic genealogies of the tribe of Judah, which establish the fundamental family lines of the people. His only role as such is to mark the genealogical continuity: son of Kenaz and brother of Othniel, he is mainly known as the father of Joab. These brief mentions fit into the project of 1 Chronicles to trace the ancestors of the chosen people and show how God preserved and organized the families of Israel.
H8304J.portee: This character reminds us that God has a people with a precise family history and genealogical continuity. Even the seemingly forgotten names in Scripture are part of God's plan for His people. The name Seraja, "the Lord reigns", affirms that divine sovereignty operates through generations and human families.

sens: Man of the tribe of Simeon during the time of the Divided Monarchy
H8304K.detail: 1. Seraja is a man of the tribe of Simeon, mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:35. He is presented as the father of Joschibia and the son of Asiel in the genealogy of Simeon. This passage lists the ancestors of a Simeonite family without providing further details about his deeds or role.
H8304K.origine: The name Seraja means "The Lord is chief" or "The Lord is master" in Hebrew. It comes from the combination of two elements: "Sar" (chief, master) and "Yah" (abbreviation of the divine name). It is a common theophoric name in the Old Testament, expressing the belief that God reigns sovereignly. Several different characters bear this name in the Bible.
H8304K.emploi: Seraja is the name of several distinct characters in the Bible: the scribe of David, a high priest under King Zedekiah at the time of the fall of Jerusalem, a man who went to Gedaliah after the exile, and others. The Seraja mentioned in 1 Chronicles 4:35 is simply a man of the tribe of Simeon whose name appears in the genealogical records of Israel, without the Bible reporting his particular actions.

sens: Man of Judah who participated in the return from exile
Chief of a priestly family during the time of Jehoiakim
Signatory of the covenant under Nehemiah
Man associated with the events of the return and the restoration of the temple
H8304L.detail: 1. Seraja is a name borne by several men in the history of Israel, notably during the return from exile in Babylon: the one who appears in the lists of returnees is a man of Judah returning with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:2). 2. One of the Seraja mentioned is a chief of a priestly family during the reign of King Jehoiakim, to whom a descendant named Meraja corresponds, showing the importance of his lineage (Nehemiah 12:12). 3. A Seraja is among those who sealed the renewed covenant with the people under the leadership of Nehemiah, demonstrating his commitment to the restored religious life of Judah (Nehemiah 10:2). 4. These references attest that Seraja was an influential man in the context of the return from exile and the reconstruction of Jerusalem.
H8304L.origine: The name Seraja means "Jehovah is prince" or "Jehovah is master", composed of two Hebrew elements: "Sera" (prince, master) and "Yah" (God). This name expresses the belief that God reigns sovereignly. Several biblical characters bear this name, reflecting a common piety at the time of the return from exile.
H8304L.emploi: Seraja appears four times in the Segond 1910, all in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, which recount the return from exile and the restoration of Jerusalem (circa 538 B.C. and after). Ezra 2:2 mentions him as one of the leaders returning with Zerubbabel. Nehemiah 10:2 and 12:1 place him among the important priests of the return. Nehemiah 12:12 reveals that he was chief of a priestly family, of which Meraja was the descendant during the reign of King Jehoiakim. These lists suggest that the Seraja cited in Ezra 2:2 is probably the same as that of Nehemiah 10:2 and 12:1, a major priestly leader of the return.

sens: Officer of King Jehoiakim of Judah
Son of Azriel
Character sent on a mission against the prophet Jeremiah
H8304M.detail:
1. Seraja is an officer of the royal court of Judah during the time of King Jehoiakim. The king entrusts him with an important mission: to arrest two men whom the monarch sees as threats (Jeremiah 36:26).
2. He is identified as the son of Azriel, which indicates his belonging to a family of the Judean elite. His status as the son of a notable explains why he is entrusted with such responsibility.
3. Along with two other men (Jerachmeel and Shelemiah), he receives the king's order to capture Baruch, the secretary, and Jeremiah, the prophet who denounces the sins of the kingdom. His role shows the conflict between royalty and the prophetic word: Seraja becomes the instrument of political power against the message of God.
H8304M.origine: The name Seraja means "the Lord is my prince" or "God is my master". In Hebrew, it comes from two roots: "sar" (prince, chief) and the divine name. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, borne by several important characters at different times. In the Judean context, it evokes a confession of faith: the one who bears this name recognizes God as his true chief, even when serving an earthly king.
H8304M.emploi: Seraja appears only once in the Segond 1910, in Jeremiah 36:26. He is mentioned there as one of the three officers sent by King Jehoiakim to arrest the prophet Jeremiah and his secretary Baruch. This passage recounts a moment of crisis: the king has just heard the reading of the scroll containing Jeremiah's words, predicting the Lord's calamities, and he is furious. He orders his officers, including Seraja, to seize those who dared to convey this message. But the text specifies that the Lord hid them—God protected His servants. Seraja embodies the resistance of political power against prophecy, but without success.

sens: Son of Neriah, officer in King Zedekiah's court
Messenger entrusted by the prophet Jeremiah to deliver a message to Babylon
H8304N.detail:
1. Seraja is a biblical figure from the time of the divided monarchy, son of Neriah and brother of Baruch. He holds a high position in King Zedekiah of Judah's court: he is the chief chamberlain, responsible for royal household affairs (Jeremiah 51:59).
2. Jeremiah chooses him as a trusted messenger to carry a written oracle against the city to Babylon (Jeremiah 51:59-61). Jeremiah commands him to publicly read these words and to throw the book into the Euphrates as a sign that Babylon will be submerged (Jeremiah 51:61).
H8304N.origine: The name Seraja means "Jehovah is master" or "Jehovah reigns." It is formed from two elements: the divine name Jehovah and a verb meaning "to dominate" or "to reign." It is a common theophoric name among the Hebrews, confessing God's sovereignty.
H8304N.emploi: Seraja appears in the book of Jeremiah during the siege of Jerusalem by Babylon. The context is dramatic: King Zedekiah surrenders to Babylon, and Seraja accompanies him. It is at this moment that Jeremiah entrusts him with his prophetic mission. The two verses that mention him report this call to be the bearer of the divine word: first his introduction as the king's companion (Jeremiah 51:59), then the command that Jeremiah gives him to read and symbolize the collapse of Babylon (Jeremiah 51:61).
H8304N.portee: Seraja embodies the faithful who accept to transmit God's word even in the most perilous circumstances. His example shows that God uses believers as messengers, even when human power seems to triumph. His mission also reveals that the prophetic word is fulfilled: it is not in vain, even when it seems impossible to accomplish.

sens: linen or hemp that has been carded and combed to untangle and align the fibers
H8305.detail: 1. The word describes linen after it has been carded and combed. This process prepares the fibers to be spun: by untangling and aligning them, a more regular and finer thread is obtained. In Isaiah 19:9, the Egyptian workers who process this combed linen — intended to make luxury white fabrics — find themselves without work, symbolizing the collapse of Egyptian prosperity.
H8305.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that refers to the idea of combing or carding. It designates the state of linen after this preparatory treatment: the fibers are cleaned, untangled, and ready for spinning.
H8305.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 19:9. The prophet describes Egypt on the eve of its divine judgment: the artisans of combed linen, who produced fine white fabrics — a prestigious and export product — will be confused, meaning deprived of their livelihood. This detail shows how judgment affects not only the great but also ordinary workers.
H8305.portee: This word reminds us that God sees every human activity, even the humble craftsmanship of processing linen. It invites us to think of God's judgment as affecting the concrete lives of people — their trades, their livelihoods, their ways of living. This makes the prophetic message more tangible and personal.

sens: Fleshy part of the body that contracts and relaxes
Physical strength, vigor of the body
H8306.detail:
1. The muscle is the fleshy and fibrous part of the body, capable of contracting to produce movement. In Job 40:11, the text describes the muscles of Behemoth's belly as the seat of its physical vigor: this is not an abstract anatomical detail, but the concrete image of the raw power of a gigantic creature.
2. By extension, muscle represents physical strength, robustness, and vital power. The mention of the belly muscles evokes here the ability to dominate, to resist, to impose one's presence — it is one of the ways the Bible speaks of domination through strength.
H8306.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁרִיר (sharir) literally designates muscle fibers, the contractile part of the body. It belongs to a family of words expressing hardness, solidity, and tension — the underlying idea is that of a taut fiber, capable of resisting and producing movement. This word reflects direct physical observation of what makes a body vigorous and capable of action.
H8306.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 40:11, where it designates the muscles of Behemoth, this mythical and colossal creature. In this context, the muscles are not simply a part of the body among others: they embody the raw and irresistible strength of this beast, placed by God as a challenge to human understanding. The unique use of the word emphasizes its highly descriptive and concrete character.
H8306.portee: This description of Behemoth's muscles invites the reader to contemplate the power of creation and its mysteries. It reminds us that extreme physical strength, even that of a fearsome creature, falls under God's dominion. For the believer, it is a call not to elevate brute strength to an absolute, but to recognize in all vigor the order established by the Creator.

sens: Obstinate inclination to do evil
Firm and stubborn resolution to follow one's own desires rather than God
Moral hardness, refusal to listen and obey
H8307.detail:
1. The word designates an inclination of the soul, a strong and persistent tendency — not a mere passing desire, but something that hardens and takes root in the heart. It is what drives someone to follow their whims without questioning: "they followed the inclinations of their heart" (Jeremiah 7:24).
2. It often involves an obstinate resolution: the person does not yield due to momentary weakness, but by a deliberate choice, even when they know it is wrong. Israel refuses to listen to God and prefers to "follow the inclinations of its evil heart" (Jeremiah 11:8), consciously and willingly.
3. This word also expresses moral closure: it is the hardening of the heart against God, the ability to resist warnings and calls to repentance. The heart becomes like rock, unyielding.
H8307.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes hardness, firmness, and obstinacy. It is related to other Hebrew words speaking of stiffness, rigidity, and inflexible resistance. The basic image is that of something hardening, becoming rigid and inaccessible — like dry wood or stone. It is not the hardness of a stable rock, but that of a will that locks itself in.
H8307.emploi: The word appears 10 times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the prophetic books and in the Law (Deuteronomy, Psalms, Jeremiah). Each occurrence describes Israel's attitude towards God: the people choose to follow the inclinations of their evil heart rather than listen to the divine voice. In Jeremiah 3:17, we see that in the future days of salvation, the people will no longer follow these inclinations; elsewhere, God notes that His people have followed them despite His warnings (Jeremiah 7:24, 9:14, 11:8). It is a diagnosis of the spiritual problem: the obstinacy of the human heart that prefers its own way.
H8307.portee: This word challenges the believer regarding the state of the heart. It reveals that sin is not a mere slip, but often a deliberate choice to follow one's desires against God's will — a gradual hardening. Understanding this term invites vigilance: to examine whether our heart is gradually locking itself in pride and disobedience. It is a call to remain open to God's voice and not to let our heart harden.

sens: That moves quickly and easily, without effort
That is swift in its movements
Character of one who runs without restraint, without holding back
H8308.detail:
1. The word primarily describes something that moves quickly and lightly. In the text of Jeremiah 2:23, the prophet compares the unfaithful nation of Israel to a "light" female dromedary in its running: it is an agile and swift creature that runs without tiring, and the word also evokes the idea of uncontrollable speed, of a wandering pace (the text says "light and wandering").
2. The meaning extends to the moral idea: a lightness of conduct, a tendency to rush into a race without direction, without holding back. In context, it is the image of Israel's unfaithfulness that "runs" after other gods, driven by a rapid and irresistible movement that it cannot control.
H8308.origine: The original Hebrew verb literally means "to twist" or "to cross" (the sense of "to entwine"). In the case of the dromedary, the idea is of movements that cross quickly, of an intertwined and wandering pace. The form used here (Piel) intensifies or actualizes this twisting movement in rapid running. The word is rare in biblical Hebrew.
H8308.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 2:23. It is applied to the dromedary to depict Israel's unfaithfulness. The prophet Jeremiah reproaches Judah for running after the Baals (the Canaanite idols) with a mad and uncontrollable impatience, like a beast that rushes without reason. The image of the "light" dromedary in its running expresses this frantic flight and moral lightness: Israel denies its unfaithfulness ("I have not defiled myself"), but its actions betray it — it moves too quickly, too easily toward sin.
H8308.portee: This word reminds us that sin is not always a struggle: sometimes, we plunge into it with a dangerous "lightness," swept away by a movement that we can no longer control. It is an invitation to self-examination: do our actions deceive us? Do we easily run toward paths that lead us away from God, without even realizing it? The image of the wandering dromedary calls us to stop and recognize our steps.

sens: a Babylonian official during the time of Nebuchadnezzar
H8310.detail: Nebu-Sar-Sékim is a high Babylonian officer, contemporary with Nebuchadnezzar II, king of Babylon. The name literally means "prince of the eunuchs," and this expression designates an important position at the royal court — one who governs the palace servants and often commands military troops as well. He appears in Jeremiah 39:3 during the fall of Jerusalem in 587 B.C., among the generals of the Babylonian king who enter the conquered city.
H8310.origine: The Babylonian name Nebu-Sar-Sékim consists of three elements: "Nebu" (the god Nebo), "Sar" (prince, chief), and "Sékîm" (eunuchs). It is a title and a proper Babylonian name, typical of the imperial court of Mesopotamia. The names of Babylonian officials are known to us from Babylonian annals and biblical documents, notably the book of Jeremiah.
H8310.emploi: Nebu-Sar-Sékim is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 39:3. At this time, Jerusalem has been besieged and starved by Nebuchadnezzar's army for several years (since 589 B.C.). The city wall is finally breached, and a delegation of high Babylonian officials enters to carry out the final operations: Rab-Sar (the supreme chief), Nebu-Sar-Sékim, Rab-Mag, and several others inspect the conquered city. His role in this text illustrates the hierarchical order of the Babylonian army.

sens: To lengthen, to make longer
To exceed a measure, to be too long
To stretch out fully, to lie down
H8311.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of lengthening something, making it longer or more extended. In Leviticus 21:18, a priest who has "a member extended" — probably an abnormally developed leg or arm — cannot approach the altar: his body exceeds the normal proportions required for the holiness of divine service.
2. The word can also mean "to exceed what is acceptable": an animal sacrifice with "a member too long" (Leviticus 22:23) will not be accepted to pay a vow, because the offering must be complete and without defect. It is an excess that disqualifies.
3. Literally, "to extend" means to lie down fully, to spread out. In Isaiah 28:20, a bed "too short to stretch out on" evokes the impossibility of finding rest: it is an image of discomfort, of unease that cannot be relieved.
H8311.origine: The verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of growth, of unfolding. The biblical context shows it applied to the body (a member that extends abnormally) and to space (to stretch out on a bed). The basic image is that of something stretching, extending beyond its natural limits.
H8311.emploi: This verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in a context of exceeding or defect. In Leviticus, the first two occurrences concern the law of priests and sacrifices: an abnormal physical defect disqualifies the priest or the sacrifice. In Isaiah 28:20, at the heart of a prophetic passage about the inadequacy of human refuges in the face of divine judgment, the bed too short symbolizes the inability to find true rest. Each time, "to extend" evokes something that exceeds the measure or cannot be contained.
H8311.portee: This word reminds us that holiness, for the ancient Israelite, was also expressed in the order of the body and physical perfection. For us today, it emphasizes that seeking rest outside of God — this is the meaning of Isaiah — will never satisfy us: we will remain "too extended" for a bed too short, uncomfortable and without true peace.

sens: Movement of the mind, idea that crosses the soul
Concern, preoccupation that troubles
Hidden intention of the heart
H8312.detail:
1. A thought is a movement of the mind, an idea that passes through our heart: in Psalms 94:19, the psalmist speaks of thoughts that stir within him, like tumultuous waves, and God comes to comfort him.
2. The word often designates a concern, a worry that troubles the soul — that which stirs and worries — for these thoughts come "in a crowd."
3. A thought can also be the secret intention of the heart, what our own conscience hides from us: in Psalms 139:23, the psalmist asks God to search his thoughts, those he does not really know himself.
H8312.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to agitate" or "to trouble" (the idea of movement and tumult). It thus primarily designates what stirs the mind, what puts it in motion — a thought, a concern. The root evokes the image of inner agitation.
H8312.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the Psalms. In Psalms 94:19, it is the agitation of thoughts that come in a crowd and trouble the believer's soul — until the consolations of God come to calm him. In Psalms 139:23, it is the most secret intention of the human heart, one that only God can scrutinize: David asks God to know his thoughts, even those that escape him. Both uses show how thoughts inhabit the heart: first as an external agitation, then as an intimate reality that only God sees.
H8312.portee: These passages remind the believer that God does not only judge our visible acts, but also knows our most hidden, most troubling thoughts. It is a call to honesty of heart before Him, and also a source of comfort: one who suffers from agitated thoughts can turn to God, the only one capable of truly knowing us and comforting us.

sens: Destroy by fire (a material, an object, or a place)
Cook by fire (bread, bricks)
Consume by fire (sacrifices, offerings)
Be reduced to ashes, disappear in flames
Reduce to nothing, annihilate (in a figurative sense)
H8313.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to make something disappear by fire: objects, clothing, entire buildings. Pharaoh "burns" the city of Gezer (1 Kings 9:16), and during the destruction of Jerusalem, the house of God and its palaces are "burned" (2 Chronicles 36:19).

2. In domestic and artisanal contexts, the word also refers to the action of cooking by fire: bricks are "cooked" by fire to serve as building materials (Genesis 11:3).

3. In Israelite worship, burning mainly concerns offerings and sacrifices: certain parts must be burned on the altar or outside the camp, such as the heart of the sacrifice or the remains that cannot be consumed (Leviticus 4:12, Leviticus 7:17).

4. The word can also have a passive subject: an object or a person "is burned," "is reduced to ashes." A fabric eaten away "will be burned by fire" (Leviticus 13:55), or the one who transgresses the covenant "will be burned by fire, he and all that belongs to him" (Joshua 7:15).

5. Metaphorically, to burn means to annihilate or completely destroy, often in a context of divine judgment or condemnation: idols and altars of false gods are burned as a sign of rupture.
H8313.origine: The Hebrew root שׂרף (saraph) expresses the primitive idea of consuming by flame. It is related to the concept of rapid and total destruction. The word appears in several forms: the simple form (Qal) means "to burn" actively, while the passive form (Niphal, Pual) means "to be burned." In Greek, the corresponding verb is καίω (kaïô), which conveys the same image of destructive fire. The root evokes an irreversible and complete action, hence its frequent use to describe divine judgment.
H8313.emploi: The verb burn appears more than 100 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Pentateuch (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy), the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles), and the prophets (Jeremiah, Isaiah). It is used in very varied ways: with legal and cultic value (what is impure or offered in sacrifice is burned), with military and destructive value (burning of cities during conquests or wars), and with spiritual value (destruction of idols and altars of false gods). The context determines the nuance: simple cooking of bread or bricks, punitive destruction, or religious purification by the elimination of evil.
H8313.portee: This verb reminds the reader that fire is the biblical instrument of definitive destruction and purification. For the Israelites, burning certain sacrifices or waste was a religious act full of meaning: it signified separating the sacred from the impure and returning to the Lord what could not remain. Spiritually, fire also evokes divine judgment that consumes evil and falsehood, reminding that God does not hesitate to destroy what transgresses His covenant.

sens: Venomous reptile whose poison causes a burning sensation
Winged fantastic creature, a kind of dragon or monster
Figure of evil and divine threat
H8314A.detail:
1. The word designates a serpent whose venom burns anyone it bites: in Numbers 21:6, the Lord sends "burning serpents" against the Israelites who complain; the bite causes intense pain, hence the name "burning."
2. In prophetic passages (Isaiah 14:29 and 30:6), the same word describes a monstrous, winged creature, a "flying dragon" — a poetic image of threatening and destructive power.
3. The burning serpent symbolizes God's judgment on sin and unbelief: it recalls divine hostility in the face of rebellion, but also the possibility of salvation through faith (in Numbers 21:8, looking at the bronze serpent heals from the bite).
H8314A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root evoking heat and burning. Its image is that of a reptile whose venom's effect resembles fire, hence the adjective "burning." The same word is also used for terrifying fantastic creatures in Near Eastern mythology.
H8314A.emploi: The word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the context of divine punishment. In Numbers 21:6-8, the burning serpents punish rebellious Israel; Moses then makes a bronze serpent that the people must look at to be healed — a foundational episode for faith in God's saving power. In Deuteronomy 8:15, Moses reminds the people of the dangers of the desert, including these serpents, to strengthen their confidence in divine protection. In Isaiah 14:29 and 30:6, the word takes on a more mythological or poetic significance: it designates a flying monster, symbol of enemy powers and chaos.
H8314A.portee: This serpent embodies both God's justified judgment on sin and the saving love of the Lord: it shows how God can transform an instrument of death into a means of salvation. For the Christian, the episode of the bronze serpent in Numbers 21:8 foreshadows Christ lifted on the cross (John 3:14) — just as one looked at the burning serpent to live, one looks at the crucified Christ to have eternal life.

sens: Celestial creature with six wings
Majestic being in the presence of God
Divine messenger bearing divine fire
H8314B.detail:
1. The seraph is a celestial creature with six wings: two to cover its face, two to cover its feet, and two to fly (Isaiah 6:2). This remarkable structure expresses both humility (covering) and mobility (flying) of this celestial being.
2. It is a majestic being that stands in direct presence of God, in His intimacy, standing around His throne. This emphasizes its high rank among the inhabitants of heaven.
3. The seraph acts as a messenger of judgment and purification: in Isaiah's vision, one of them flies to the prophet holding a burning stone taken from the altar, symbol of divine fire and holiness (Isaiah 6:6).
H8314B.origine: The Hebrew word "saraph" comes from a root meaning "to burn." The seraph is therefore literally a "burning" or "fiery" being, reflecting either its nature of pure fire or its proximity to the divine fire of God's presence. This name describes a creature defined by its ardor, energy, and relationship to the sacred fire.
H8314B.emploi: The word appears only twice, both in the inaugural vision of the prophet Isaiah in chapter 6. This is the major appearance of seraphim in Hebrew Scripture. They form a distinct category of celestial beings, different from cherubim: while cherubim guard and protect, seraphim worship God around His throne and execute His judgments. Their presence in Isaiah's vision is highly symbolic: they sing of God's holiness and purify the prophet for his missionary calling.
H8314B.portee: The vision of the seraphim reminds the believer of the reality of the living presence of God surrounded by celestial beings who worship Him. It invites meditation on the absolute holiness of God and the purifying fire of His presence. For the reader of Isaiah, this image reveals that even in exile or distress, God reigns gloriously, worshiped by His heavenly court.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, son of Chela
H8315.detail: Saraph is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible. He was the son of Chela and brother of Er, Laada, Jokim, and Joash. According to the account in 1 Chronicles 4:22, Saraph and Jokim, along with other men from Cozeba, ruled over Moab during the time of Egypt and the desert — an ancient period whose exact historicity remains obscure.
H8315.origine: The name Saraph (שָׂרָף) literally means "to burn" in Hebrew, from the verb ש-ר-פ which expresses the action of consuming by fire. This name may evoke a character trait or a lineage known for its strength or authority. It is a typical patronymic in the genealogy of Judah transmitted in Chronicles.
H8315.emploi: Saraph appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:22. This mention places him in a genealogical context: he is listed among the descendants of Judah, specifically in the branch of Chela. The text indicates that he "ruled over Moab" with Jokim and other men from Cozeba, suggesting a position of power or authority in a distant time in Israel's history.

sens: Intense fire that burns and consumes
Action of burning, reducing to ashes
Destruction by fire
Intense fervor or passion
H8316.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a vivid fire that actively burns: in Genesis 11:3, men bake bricks in the fire to build the Tower of Babel.
2. It evokes the action of reducing something to ashes by fire: in Numbers 19:17, ashes from the victim that has been burned in the atonement ceremony are taken.
3. It is used to speak of massive destruction by fire: in Jeremiah 51:25, God transforms a mountain into a blazing mountain, meaning completely given over to flames and destruction.
4. In the context of worship or honor, it describes the perfumes and spices that are solemnly burned: in 2 Chronicles 16:14, a very considerable amount of perfumes is burned in honor of the king, where the fire symbolizes the respect given.
H8316.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of burning and consuming. It is related to other biblical words concerning fire and combustion. In Hebrew, this term is regularly used to describe fire in both a literal and figurative sense, particularly in contexts of divine judgment or destruction.
H8316.emploi: The word appears about twelve times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (Chronicles) and prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos). It is first used for the concrete fire used in rituals or construction: baking bricks (Genesis 11:3), atonement ceremony (Numbers 19:6-17). It also describes sacred fires whose ashes must be preserved (Numbers 16:37). In prophetic passages, it becomes an image of destruction and divine judgment: blazing mountain (Jeremiah 51:25), warrior garments given to the flames (Isaiah 9:4). It is a word from concrete vocabulary that easily ascends to the figurative sense of total destruction.
H8316.portee: This word reminds us that God controls fire, an instrument of judgment and purification. It invites the reader to take prophetic warnings seriously: the fire of God consumes what opposes His will. In the rituals of the Old Testament, the blazing purified; it is an image of how God cleanses and renews His people.

sens: To move by crawling on the ground, referring to small animals or reptiles
To proliferate, to multiply in large numbers
To spread, to extend over a surface or territory
To swarm, to teem with living creatures
H8317.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of small animals that move by crawling on the ground: reptiles, insects, creatures that have no legs or have few. In Leviticus 11:41, Moses forbids eating "any creeping thing that crawls on the earth," a category of animals deemed unclean according to the Law.

2. The word also denotes proliferation, multiplication in large numbers: creeping creatures reproduce quickly and invade spaces. In Exodus 1:7, the Israelites in Egypt "multiplied" (the text uses the same word), spreading throughout the land.

3. In Genesis 9:7, after the Flood, God commands Noah and his sons: "Be fruitful and multiply on the earth," meaning occupy and populate the whole world by dispersing.

4. The image becomes one of swarming, an abundance that covers everything: in Exodus 7:28, the Nile "will swarm with frogs" during the plague, suggesting an invasion, an overwhelming abundance.
H8317.origine: The Hebrew root fundamentally means "to move by crawling." It evokes the image of small creatures that populate the ground and waters: reptiles, insects, aquatic creatures. The word belongs to the realm of animal creation, of the living beings "that creep" (in Hebrew, they are called the "שְׁרָצִים", shérats). In Genesis, it is this same root that names the first wave of animal creation, that of creatures that swarm and proliferate.
H8317.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Pentateuch (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus). In Genesis 1:20-21, God commands the waters to "bring forth abundantly" living creatures, establishing a category of created beings. In Leviticus 11, it rules over the "creeping" animals declared unclean. In Exodus, the verb describes the plagues (the frogs that swarm). In Genesis 9:7 and Exodus 1:7, it takes the meaning of "to multiply and spread." Psalm 105:30 and Ezekiel 47:9 continue to use it to express the proliferation of creatures or life that swarms. The context varies: creation, ritual purity, plagues, multiplication of peoples.
H8317.portee: This word reminds the believer that God created all life, including the humblest creatures that crawl. It also questions the purity and boundaries that God sets (the Law distinguishes between clean and unclean animals). Finally, when applied to humans, it expresses the divine order of fruitfulness and dominion over the earth: to multiply is not an accident, it is a blessing and a command.

sens: Small animal that crawls or moves in large numbers
Small aquatic or terrestrial creature
Animal declared unclean by the Law of Moses
H8318.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to tiny or modest creatures that move by crawling or dragging themselves — insects, small reptiles, creatures that move in a characteristic way. The image is one of a swarming multitude: in Genesis 1:20, God says that the waters produce living creatures in "abundance," evoking both profusion and continuous movement.
2. The word particularly applies to small aquatic or terrestrial creatures, as opposed to large animals. In Leviticus 11:10, it speaks of the reptiles of the sea and rivers, distinct from fish and larger creatures.
3. In the Law of Moses, the reptile becomes a ritual category: these creatures are declared unclean. Touching a dead reptile renders one unclean until evening (Leviticus 11:31), and eating them is forbidden (Leviticus 11:42). This impurity is linked to their humble and degraded nature, considered contrary to the holiness that God demands from His people.
H8318.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of swarming, teeming, moving in mass — the characteristic movement of a multitude of small creatures. The root is related to the image of a living and moving abundance. The word applies to the creatures "that creep," to all beings that crawl or move low on the ground.
H8318.emploi: This word appears fifteen times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the purity laws of Leviticus (more than ten times) and at the beginning of Genesis. In Genesis 1:20 and 7:21, the word simply refers to the countless aquatic creatures that God creates. But starting from Leviticus 5 and especially Leviticus 11, the context becomes legal and religious: the reptile becomes the figure of ritual impurity, a creature whose contact or consumption defiles anyone who touches it. The repetitions in Leviticus 11:20-44 emphasize the Law's insistence: these animals must be held in abomination. The meaning oscillates between the simple tiny creature and the religious symbol of what is unclean.
H8318.portee: For the believer, the word "reptile" in the Law reveals how God establishes boundaries between the clean and the unclean, the acceptable and the unacceptable — not arbitrarily, but to form a holy people. These dietary prohibitions, though abolished in Christ (Mark 7:19), remind us that holiness begins with vigilance: what we receive in our body and our life is not indifferent. They also teach that God classifies all creatures according to an order, and that our obedience involves respecting that order.

sens: to emit a high-pitched sound by passing air between the lips or teeth
to call someone or an animal by whistling
to express disdain, astonishment, or mockery through a whistle
to gather or summon by a sound signal
H8319.detail:
1. To whistle means to produce a high-pitched sound with the mouth: it is a distinct and audible human noise. In Isaiah 5:26, the Lord "whistles" to call a distant people, just as one whistles to summon someone.
2. Whistling can be a call or a signal: Zechariah 10:8 says, "I will call them by whistling," to gather His people as one gathers a flock.
3. Very often, whistling expresses disdain and mockery: in Lamentations 2:16, the enemies "whistle" at defeated Jerusalem; in 1 Kings 9:8, passersby whistle at the destroyed temple, as one whistles at a shameful ruin.
4. Whistling can also express astonishment and horror at desolation: in Jeremiah 50:13, those passing by ruined Babylon "whistle" in astonishment, accompanying this gesture with disdain.
H8319.origine: The Hebrew word sharah comes from a root that imitates the sound of whistling itself (onomatopoeia). This root is close to other Hebrew words denoting high or piercing sounds. Whistling was a known social gesture: a call signal among shepherds and hunters, but also a gesture of derision towards the defeated or the fallen.
H8319.emploi: This verb appears 12 times in the Old Testament, concentrated in the prophets of doom (Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel) and the minor prophets (Zephaniah, Zechariah). It is first used in the literal sense: to call by whistling (Isaiah 5:26, Zechariah 10:8). But it mainly takes on an ironic and contemptuous meaning: to express disdain towards ruined cities and kingdoms (Babylon in Jeremiah 50:13, Jerusalem in Lamentations 2:16). Whistling thus becomes a gesture of insult that enemies direct at the defeated. Job 27:23 uses it for the contempt that men express towards a wicked person. This word paints the public shame of divine judgment.
H8319.portee: Whistling reminds us that God's judgment on guilty cities exposes the guilty to mockery and public humiliation. It is a word that gives the human measure of ruin: not only material destruction but also the affront and disdain of witnesses. For the believer, it warns of the real cost of unfaithfulness — not only loss but also shame. Conversely, the call by whistling (Zechariah) evokes the grace that gathers: the same gesture that insults the wicked can become a summons for the forgiven people.

sens: reddish or brownish color, leaning towards russet
Coat of an animal, especially a horse, that has this hue
A resplendent or imposing appearance marked by this color
H8320.detail:
1. The word "reddish-brown" designates a color between russet and brown, leaning towards red or orange — the hue of fire or copper. In Zechariah 1:8, the prophet sees in his night vision horses that are "reddish-brown," of a beautiful reddish color that makes them remarkable and imposing.
2. Applied to an animal, the word speaks of its coat, that is, the color of its fur or hair. The reddish-brown horse in Zechariah 1:8 is distinguished by its distinctive hue among other horses (white, brown, or black).
3. The reddish-brown color also suggests power and energy — a striking and brilliant appearance, suitable for the mount of a warrior or a divine messenger in a celestial vision.
H8320.origine: The Hebrew word שָׂרֹק (saruq) belongs to a family of Hebrew words related to reddish hues and fire. It evokes the image of a color that burns or shines, reminiscent of polished copper or flame. This term is rare in the Old Testament and mainly characterizes the distinctive coat of horses, symbols of power and swift movement.
H8320.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Zechariah 1:8. It describes the horses in a prophetic vision — divine or angelic mounts with remarkable colors. This unique occurrence makes it a specialized word, used to paint a mysterious and symbolic scene: in the prophet's vision, the horses of different colors (reddish, white) constitute a celestial procession. The reddish-brown hue gives these horses a majestic and supernatural appearance, worthy of a theophany or divine manifestation.
H8320.portee: This vision of the reddish-brown horses reminds the reader that God remains active and vigilant over the world, even in spiritual darkness. The reddish-brown horses, with their striking color and power, symbolize the divine presence and its hidden action. This image invites the believer to recognize that God sees all and acts constantly, even when we do not see Him.

sens: A species of vine known for the exceptional quality of its grapes
Plant or grape produced by this vine
Biblical image of the people of Israel, planted by God to bear fruit
H8321A.detail:
1. The word designates a particular variety of vine, cultivated to produce tasty and high-quality grapes. In Isaiah 5:2, the vineyard owner plants a "choice vine" that he surrounds with all care: he removes the stones, builds a tower, digs a vat. It is an elite vine, not left to chance.
2. By extension, the term can refer to the grapes or the fruit produced by this exceptional vine. The quality of the plant determines the flavor of the harvest.
3. Biblically, Jeremiah 2:21 uses this image to speak of Israel: "I had planted you like a choice vine and a seed of highest quality." God chose Israel, established it with care, expecting good moral and spiritual fruit. This choice vine ultimately degenerates, which explains the Lord's disappointment.
H8321A.origine: The Hebrew word שֹׂרֵק (sorèq) literally designates a superior quality plant. It is related to the idea of selection and excellence. As a noun, it evokes both the noble plant and the grape it produces. The image of a vine planted with care by a attentive owner often recurs in prophetic poetry to speak of God's relationship with His people.
H8321A.emploi: The word appears twice in the Old Testament. In Isaiah 5:2, it characterizes the vine planted by the vineyard master, which will be the subject of divine judgment at the heart of an oracle: God has given Israel all advantages, and yet it bears only bad fruit (sour grapes). In Jeremiah 2:21, the prophet reminds Israel that God had planted it as a "choice vine," but the nation has transformed into a "foreign vine" — it has degenerated and strayed from its calling. The context of both passages is always that of divine reproach towards the unfaithful people.
H8321A.portee: This powerful image reminds the believer that God chooses His people not by chance, but with intention and tenderness, expecting them to bear spiritual fruit — justice, wisdom, obedience. When Israel "degenerates," it is a tragedy, because it had received so many graces. The word invites each generation of believers to ask themselves: what do I bear in my life? Have I become a sweet or bitter grape?

sens: Exceptional quality vine plant
Symbol of prosperity and fertility
Wealth and abundance in divine blessing
H8321B.detail:
1. The word refers to a chosen vine plant, selected for its superior quality. In Genesis 49:11, Judah is blessed with a best vine: the image evokes someone who possesses not only the vineyard but the finest plants, those that produce the most precious grapes. It is the vineyard of the wealthy, one that requires care and yields abundantly.
2. This best vine becomes an image of prosperity and blessing. Tying his donkey to the vine means having so much wealth that one can afford to be generous. Judah reigns in peace, to the point that he never lacks grapes and wine, having enough to wash his clothes in wine—a picture of extraordinary luxury and abundance.
3. More broadly, the quality vine symbolizes the divine blessing that fills the heart and life: having a best vine means receiving from God not just the bare minimum, but excellence and generosity.
H8321B.origine: The Hebrew word שֹׂרֵק (sorèq) comes from a root that evokes quality and choice. It refers to a particular species of vine, renowned for its excellent grapes. It is not just any vine, but one that is chosen and carefully cultivated. The form שֹׂרֵקָה (sorèqah) is a feminine variant of the same word.
H8321B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 49:11, in the blessing that Jacob pronounces over his son Judah. Jacob paints an idealized portrait of the tribe of Judah: a leader who reigns in peace and abundance, surrounded by so much agricultural wealth that he can tie his donkey to precious vines. This image of fertility and inexhaustible prosperity characterizes the royal blessing intended for the house of Judah.
H8321B.portee: This word of blessing reminds the reader that true prosperity does not come from luck or personal effort alone, but from divine blessing. To possess a best vine is to enjoy the abundant gifts that God pours out on those He elevates. It also invites recognition that blessing is not merely a metaphor: it manifests concretely in life, rest, and joy.

sens: the hissing or derisive noise made against someone or something
the state of being the object of ridicule and public contempt
a situation that provokes scandal and outrage among those who witness it
H8322.detail:
1. The word first paints the concrete image of mocking hissing: it is the noise made to express disdain or indignation (see Jeremiah 19:8, where passersby "will hiss at all its wounds"). It is the gesture of disdain.
2. From there, it designates the one or that which is the object of it: the person or thing that has become the subject of ridicule. When a people or a city becomes a "mockery" (2 Chronicles 29:8, Jeremiah 25:18), it has lost all dignity in the eyes of others.
3. More broadly, the word describes a state of public infamy, where humiliation accompanies material ruin. Babylon becomes "a desolation and a mockery" (Jeremiah 51:37): it is no longer an empire, but a place pointed at with disdain.
H8322.origine: The word comes from the root שׁרק (šāraq), which means "to hiss." The hissing is its primary image: it is the natural sound of contempt. The feminine noun in Hebrew (šeréqāh) somewhat personifies this mockery as a force exercised against a people.
H8322.emploi: The word appears seven times in the Old Testament, always in the prophets or later historical accounts. It is used primarily by Jeremiah (five occurrences: Jeremiah 19:8, 25:9, 25:18, 29:18, 51:37) to describe the punishment of nations that turn away from God. In these passages, mockery is added to other plagues: desolation, curse, disgrace. It is the fate reserved for Judah, Jerusalem, and Babylon. The context is always that of divine judgment: when a people transgresses, God makes them a spectacle of ignominy. The word never denotes a mere joke, but the public humiliation of an entire nation.
H8322.portee: This word reminds the reader that God's judgment is not limited to material destruction: it includes shame, loss of reputation, and dignity. To see a nation reduced to mockery is to see the order of the world overturned. For the believer, this warns that obeying God preserves honor, while rebellion exposes one to shame. It is also a call to fear God: to avoid becoming oneself an object of mockery in the eyes of the nations.

sens: To exercise authority over a people or territory
To dominate, to have power over someone
To command, to reign with justice
To direct public affairs
H8323A.detail:
1. To govern means to exercise royal or political authority over a people or territory. The word evokes the role of the king or prince who leads the nation. In Isaiah 32:1, the king "will govern according to justice," which shows that to govern is to lead responsibly.

2. To dominate expresses the idea of having power and authority over someone, often in a stronger or imposed manner. In Numbers 16:13, Korah reproaches Moses for "continuing to dominate" over the people, emphasizing the exercise of power.

3. To command and to reign denote sovereign authority: the king or leader gives orders and others obey. In Proverbs 8:16, Wisdom says that it is by her that "the chiefs govern" and that "the judges of the earth judge."

4. To direct public affairs suggests active management of the interests of the people or household. In Esther 1:22, every man must be "master in his house," meaning he has the authority and responsibility to direct it.
H8323A.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׂרַר (sarar) comes from a root that carries the idea of domination and authority. It is close to the word שַׂר (sar, "prince" or "chief"), showing that to govern is the action of the prince. The root evokes the power of the one who reigns, whether king, magistrate, or head of household. This verb belongs to the family of Hebrew words describing authority and command.
H8323A.emploi: The verb שָׂרַר appears four times in the Old Testament, in contexts of political or domestic authority. In Numbers 16:13, it describes the power that Moses exercises over Israel and which is contested. In Esther 1:22, it designates the authority of the husband over his household. In Proverbs 8:16 and Isaiah 32:1, it applies to kings and princes who govern the nation. The word is used for both just authority and abused authority, depending on the context.
H8323A.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the nature of authority: to govern is not just to have power, but also to exercise it with justice and responsibility. Isaiah 32:1 shows that true governance rests on justice, while Numbers 16:13 reminds us that all power can be contested. For the Christian, to govern calls for serving rather than arbitrarily dominating.

sens: one who is hostile, who shows enmity
one who fights, who persecutes
one who is feared or distrusted
H8324.detail:
1. An enemy is someone who shows hostility towards a person, who wishes them harm. It is the opposite of a friend: instead of seeking good, the enemy seeks to do harm. The psalmist asks God to lead him in righteousness "because of his enemies" (Psalms 5:9), for righteousness protects him against those who wish him ill.
2. The enemy is one who actively persecutes, harasses, and makes war. In the Psalms, adversaries "harass" the believer "all day long" and "make war against him like the proud" (Psalms 56:3) — these are adversaries who act, who attack.
3. Beyond physical combat, the enemy also represents one whom the believer fears or dreads. But God can transform this feeling: the psalmist pleads with God to "make him see with joy those who persecute him" (Psalms 59:11), asking that fear be turned into joy through trust in God.
H8324.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of being hostile, showing enmity. It is an active word: the enemy is not simply someone who is disliked, but someone who acts against you, who persecutes you. The root also evokes the idea of showing oneself as an adversary, facing with hostility.
H8324.emploi: This word appears five times in the Psalms, always in prayers where the psalmist asks God to protect him from his enemies. It is used in the concrete sense of adversaries who fight, persecute, and harass the believer (Psalms 56:3). In all the uses in the Psalms, the enemy is one who threatens the righteous, and the psalmist calls upon God to be delivered, guided, or protected. The word thus expresses an active and enduring hostility, not a mere momentary opposition.
H8324.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us of a reality: we can have enemies, adversaries who wish us harm or persecute us. But the Psalms show that the reaction is not personal vengeance — it is to call upon God, to ask Him for protection and justice. The word also invites us to trust: even in the face of numerous and relentless enemies, God guides us and can transform our fear into joy through the certainty of His support.

sens: man from the time of the united monarchy, father of the warrior Ahiam
H8325.detail: Scharar is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the time of King David. He is known as the father of Ahiam, who is listed among David's mighty warriors in 2 Samuel 23:33. The text identifies him by his patronymic: Ahiam is "the son of Scharar, of Arar," meaning he comes from this family.
H8325.origine: The name Scharar likely means "enemy" in Hebrew. It is also found in the form Sachar (or Sacar according to some variants) in the parallel list of 1 Chronicles 11:35. These variants reflect slightly different textual traditions of the same character or family.
H8325.emploi: Scharar appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 23:33, in the list of David's most valiant warriors. He is identified as the father of Ahiam, who held the title of mighty warrior in the king's service. His existence is known only through this familial link and military context.

sens: The navel, this small depression at the center of the abdomen from which the umbilical cord originated
In a figurative sense, that which is central, intimate, and precious
H8326.detail:
1. The navel refers to the belly button, this physical mark on the human body that recalls the original link with the mother. In the Song of Solomon, the poet describes the beloved's body by comparing it to a rounded cup, an image of beauty and delicacy (Song of Solomon 7:3).
2. Just as the navel is at the heart of the body, the word can evoke what is central, intimate, that which touches the essence of a person. In the biblical poet's view, this delicate allusion transforms a simple part of the body into a symbol of grace and seduction.
H8326.origine: The Hebrew word שׁוֹרֶר (shorèr) primarily designates the navel, this small scar where the umbilical cord once attached. Its etymology brings us back to the image of the link with life itself. In biblical language, this word belongs to the vocabulary of the human body in its most concrete and intimate realities.
H8326.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in the Song of Solomon 7:3, a poetic text that celebrates the beauty of the body. The context shows that the poet chooses his words carefully to evoke images that are both sensual and delicate: he compares the navel to a round cup filled with fragrant wine, transforming an anatomical reality into a symbol of feminine grace.
H8326.portee: This passage from the Song of Solomon reminds us that the Bible does not shy away from speaking of the human body and sensual beauty, not as a shame, but as part of creation. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation to recognize that God created man and woman in their physical integrity, and that celebrating this beauty in a context of mutual love reflects God's design.

sens: To establish or form roots in the ground
To uproot a plant by its roots
To gain solidity, to consolidate and expand
To destroy or annihilate something definitively
H8327.detail:
1. To establish or form roots: this is the action of a plant that drives its roots into the soil to nourish and stabilize itself. Isaiah 27:6 speaks of Jacob who "will take root," meaning Israel will firm up and flourish like a plant that grows deep.
2. To uproot a plant by its roots: this means to completely remove it, taking away what holds the plant in the ground. Job 31:8 wishes that his "offspring be uprooted," an expression of total curse.
3. To gain solidity and expand: beyond mere growth, it means to become strong, stable, and prosperous. Psalm 80:10 describes how God makes room for a vine that "throws down roots and fills the land."
4. To destroy definitively: in a figurative sense, to completely annihilate, like God who "will uproot" his enemy from the land of the living (Psalms 52:7), meaning He will erase them forever.
H8327.origine: The word comes from the root שׁרשׁ which originally designates the root of a plant, that underground part which holds and nourishes it. The verb naturally derives from it, expressing the action of forming, fixing, or removing roots. This image of rooting was familiar to the agricultural peoples of Israel, where the prosperity of a household or lineage was often compared to that of a well-rooted tree.
H8327.emploi: The verb appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Psalms and Isaiah. In Job, it first designates the bad fate of a harvest doomed to be uprooted. In the Psalms, it expresses either the stability and blessing of a plant that God protects (Psalm 80), or the destruction of one He judges (Psalm 52). Isaiah uses it to paint the future renewal of Israel that "will take root." The meaning constantly shifts between the botanical image and its spiritual or political application: to root is to strengthen, and to uproot is to annihilate.
H8327.portee: This word teaches that solidity and prosperity come from a deep planting: God blesses those who root themselves in Him, who draw their strength from a firm foundation. Conversely, being "uprooted" by God is the image of total destruction, exile, irrevocable judgment. For the believer, the image invites us to seek deep roots in faith rather than relying on fragile appearances.

sens: Underground part of a plant that absorbs water and nutrients from the soil
Foundation, base from which everything depends
Origin, lineage of a family or a people
Stability, solidity, or permanence of a person or a nation
H8328.detail:
1. The root is primarily the part of a plant buried underground that nourishes and sustains it: in Job 14:8, it speaks of the root that ages in the ground, and in Ezekiel 17:9, it mentions the uprooting of roots that destroys the entire plant.
2. Figuratively, the root becomes the foundation or starting point: Isaiah 37:31 describes what "will put down roots below," suggesting that the plant (a restored people) starts anew from the base, establishing a new foundation.
3. The root symbolizes the origin of a family or a people, its primary lineage, from which it descends: it refers to root in the sense of lineage or heritage.
4. It also expresses strength, stability, and permanence: a deep root signifies a nation or person firmly established. But a rotten or uprooted root signifies ruin: Isaiah 5:24 shows that the root of an unfaithful people "will be like rottenness," announcing its collapse.
H8328.origine: The Hebrew word for root (שֹׁרֶשׁ) comes from a family of words evoking stability and foundation. Its primary image is that of the root of a tree embedded in the ground, from which it draws its sustenance. This word is used throughout the Old Testament to describe both plants (its concrete uses) and, transposed, the solidity of peoples and individuals: a nation with deep roots can survive and bear fruit.
H8328.emploi: The word appears 32 times in biblical Hebrew, mainly in the wisdom books (Job, Proverbs) and among the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah, Hosea). In a literal context, it designates the underground part of plants and trees. In a figurative and prophetic context, it becomes a powerful image: the root of a person or a people represents their moral solidity, their ability to endure and produce spiritual fruit. Isaiah speaks of one who "will put down roots" to show restoration after judgment; Malachi mentions roots that will be burned to describe final judgment. The context always indicates whether the root is healthy and life-giving, or rotten and destined for destruction.
H8328.portee: For the believer, the image of the root reminds us of the importance of a solid foundation in faith: having deep roots in the Word of God and in the knowledge of God ensures spiritual stability and fruitfulness. It also warns of the danger of losing one's roots, of drifting away from the received foundation. This image unites lasting stability with the ability to bear fruit, showing that true spiritual growth depends on well-planted roots.

sens: Man of the tribe of Manasseh, son of Machir
H8329.detail: Scheresh is a man of the tribe of Manasseh, mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the son of Machir and Maacah, himself the grandson of Manasseh. He had brothers (Gilead, Peresh, and Hammoleketh) and sons (Ulam and Rekem) who are listed in the genealogy of Manasseh in 1 Chronicles 7:16.
H8329.origine: The name Scheresh comes from the Hebrew שָׁרֶשׁ (sheresh), which literally means "root." This word evokes the idea of a root that sinks into the ground and from which the plant grows; applied to a man, it can suggest a person who is the source or origin of a lineage. In the Old Testament, sheresh is used literally to speak of the roots of plants, and figuratively to designate origins or foundations.
H8329.emploi: Scheresh is mentioned only once in the biblical genealogies, in 1 Chronicles 7:16. He appears in the genealogical list of the tribe of Manasseh, where he is presented as the son of Machir and Maacah, and as the father of Ulam and Rekem. His role in biblical history is limited to this presence in the genealogical records of the sons of Israel, which shows his importance in the continuity of the Manasseh lineage.

sens: The underground part of a tree or plant that sinks into the ground
Figuratively: what remains of a fallen power, what can allow for restoration
H8330.detail:
1. The root is the part of a tree that sinks underground and nourishes it. In the dream of Nebuchadnezzar reported in Daniel, the tree is cut down, but its roots are left in the ground with the trunk, bound by chains (Daniel 4:15) — the concrete image of a plant that can be reborn if its roots survive.
2. Figuratively, the root represents what remains of a reign or power that appears to be destroyed. When the prophet Daniel explains the dream, he tells the king that leaving the roots means that his kingdom will remain, for God will keep this living foundation (Daniel 4:26) — a word of hope in judgment.
H8330.origine: This Aramaic word (שֹׁרֶשׁ) is very close to its Hebrew equivalent (שֹׁרֶשׁ, H8328), as these sister languages share the same root. The starting image is simple: what grips, what holds firm. The word evokes both underground stability and the ability to be reborn.
H8330.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Aramaic Bible, exclusively in chapter 4 of the book of Daniel, in the interpretation of the dream of the great tree. In Daniel 4:15 and 4:23, it designates the literal roots that must be left intact when the tree is cut down. In Daniel 4:26, the prophet uses it symbolically: leaving the roots means that God preserves the foundations of the king's reign, promising restoration after judgment. This is a passage where the concrete (the physical roots) shifts to the spiritual sense (the permanence of power).
H8330.portee: This image of the roots left in the ground speaks to the heart of the believer confronted with trial or judgment.
